title: Sultanate of Maguindanao
capsule: The Sultanate of Maguindanao was an Islamic polity on the island of Mindanao in the southern Philippines, traditionally traced to Sharif Kabungsuwan, a Muslim missionary from Johor who married into local ruling families and spread Islam through the Pulangi (Cotabato) River valley in the early sixteenth century. At its height under Sultan Kudarat (r. c. 1619-1671) the sultanate repelled repeated Spanish attempts to subdue the Cotabato basin, allied with the Sulu Sultanate and Ternate, and projected influence across much of Mindanao. Its wealth rested on trade in rice, wax, and forest products and on a maritime raiding economy in which Iranun and Maranao fleets supplied captives to regional slave markets. Through the eighteenth and into the nineteenth century it remained the dominant Muslim power of the Pulangi region, negotiating and clashing with the Spanish presence in the south.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Core territory in the Cotabato basin is reasonably attested in Spanish colonial records, but the sultanate's outer boundary — especially tributary zones in upland Mindanao — fluctuated considerably and is imprecisely mapped.
